raw_response:
I've been working this land for 30 years. My back knows every corner of it. Twenty-point-eight mu — not big, but it's ours. My daughter went to work in Shijiazhuang last year, so we're down one pair of hands, but my husband is still here and we manage.

We do wheat-maize, same as everyone in Quzhou. All 20.8 mu goes to wheat in the fall, then we turn it over to maize right after the June harvest. No spare land, no gaps. That's just how the season runs here.

**Wheat:** I buy the improved variety from the township seed station — same one I've used for five or six years now. It's not the fanciest seed but I know how it behaves on my soil and that matters more to me than what some technician says is better. Before planting in October I'll rotary till and put down base fertilizer — compound fertilizer plus some urea. In spring, when the wheat starts to joint, I'll topdress with more urea. I water three times usually: once before the ground freezes to help the roots set, once at jointing, once at heading. If grain fill looks dry I'll add a fourth. I spray herbicide in spring — broadleafs come up every year along the edges. I'll watch for rust; if I see yellow patches I spray again. Two pesticide runs most years.

**Maize:** Hybrid seed, definitely. I've been buying hybrid maize for maybe fifteen years now. The yields are just better, there's no argument. After wheat comes off — late June usually — we rotary till right away and get seed in the ground within a week. There's no time to waste. I fertilize at planting and topdress once when it's knee-high. Irrigation twice at minimum — silking is critical, I never skip that one, and again at grain fill if the well holds. Corn borer shows up some years so I spray for that, and herbicide right after emergence. Two applications.

I'm not experimenting this year. Prices for both grain are uncertain and one bad season hurts us badly. I'll do what worked last year.
